strings.name: Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim
strings.role: Chadian Indigenous-rights and climate advocate; president of AFPAT
strings.summary: Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim comes from Chad’s Mbororo pastoralist community and advocates bringing Indigenous knowledge, women’s rights and climate adaptation into public decisions. She helped establish and leads AFPAT, combining participatory community mapping with international advocacy. She became a UN Sustainable Development Goals Advocate in 2019 and chaired the 2024 session of the Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026. Recent records include receiving an award in Monaco in October and publishing a signed article on 9 November. Contemporary sources support her AFPAT presidency. Her chairmanship of the UN Forum’s 2024 session is not presented as a current 2026 office; policy proposals in her article are attributed to her.
strings.influence.rationale: She represents African Indigenous communities in international climate and biodiversity discussions, bringing traditional knowledge and women’s rights into policy debates.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and community background
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in 1984 in N’Djamena, Chad, she belongs to the Mbororo Fulani pastoralist community. Her mother supported schooling for her children, an experience that also shaped Ibrahim’s interest in women’s education and community rights.
strings.facts.f2.label: Participatory mapping
strings.facts.f2.value: She brings herders, farmers and other community members together to identify water sources, pastoral routes and natural resources. The work combines local ecological knowledge with 2D and 3D geographical tools to inform land management, resource negotiations and climate adaptation.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Knowledge and resource governance
strings.highlights.h1.text: She advocates recognizing Indigenous peoples as knowledge holders and decision makers and directing climate finance to local communities. Mapping can facilitate discussion of resource needs; project accounts of reduced conflict and advocacy goals do not substitute for independent evaluation or a full analysis of regional conflict.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Women’s rights and community participation
strings.highlights.h2.text: AFPAT connects women’s education, health, access to justice and environmental protection. Ibrahim advocates women’s participation in community discussions and international cooperation grounded in local knowledge, rights and consent. Her work connects pastoral communities’ everyday needs with global climate-governance debates.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Receives the Planetary Health Award for Awareness
strings.timeline.t1.text: Honoured in the Awareness category at the Prince Albert II of Monaco Foundation’s awards ceremony for advocacy on Indigenous rights and traditional ecological knowledge. The event took place on 16 October; the foundation published its release on 17 October. Other laureates’ scientific and technological achievements are not attributed to her.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Elected chair of the UN Forum session
strings.timeline.t2.text: Elected chair at the first meeting of the twenty-third session of the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. The role is recorded by session: Aluki Kotierk was the chair presenting the twenty-fifth-session report in 2026, so Ibrahim’s older title must not be carried forward.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Named a Rolex Awards for Enterprise laureate
strings.timeline.t3.text: One of the 2021 laureates for using Indigenous knowledge in resource mapping and climate adaptation. Her project combines community knowledge with modern geographical methods. The award year is distinct from the later publication of the project profile.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Wins the Pritzker Emerging Environmental Genius Award
strings.timeline.t4.text: UCLA’s Institute of the Environment and Sustainability presented its 2019 award, with a US$100,000 prize, supporting her Indigenous and environmental work. This is an environmental-innovation award, not the Pritzker Architecture Prize. The report was published the following day.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Appointed an SDG Advocate
strings.timeline.t5.text: One of six new SDG Advocates appointed by the UN secretary-general to advance the 2030 Agenda. The appointments brought the group to 17 members at the time; this did not make her an executive head of the UN Secretariat.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Becomes a senior Indigenous fellow at Conservation International
strings.timeline.t6.text: The UN Office for Partnerships biography records her as a senior Indigenous fellow at Conservation International from 2018, linking community ecological knowledge with international conservation discussions. This is an institutional role, not a university degree.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Speaks at the Paris Agreement signing ceremony
strings.timeline.t7.text: Addressed the ceremony at UN Headquarters in New York as a civil-society representative, calling for more adaptation funding and attention to impacts on communities in Chad. The location was New York; speaking for civil society was not signing the treaty on behalf of a state.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Helps establish AFPAT
strings.timeline.t8.text: Helped create the Association for Indigenous Women and Peoples of Chad to promote community rights and environmental protection. Both a 2015 interview and UNESCO’s 2019 interview distinguish its creation from gaining legal status in 2005; registration was not the beginning of the initiative.
